title: The Sixth River
subtitle: The Partition of British India: Delhi, Karachi, Lahore, Calcutta, June–November 1947
intro: On 3 June 1947 the Viceroy and three Indian leaders went on the radio to announce that British India would be divided. Ten weeks later, on 14 and 15 August, Pakistan and India became independent. The line between them in the Punjab and Bengal was not published until 17 August. In the months that followed, somewhere between ten and fifteen million people crossed the new borders. Hindus and Sikhs moved east, Muslims moved west and, in Bengal, people moved in both directions. Estimates of the dead run from a few hundred thousand to around a million, and the violence fell on every community.

The Urdu writer Fikr Taunsvi called his Lahore journal The Sixth River: the Punjab already had five rivers, and Partition added a river of blood. His is one of very few true diaries kept by an ordinary participant as events happened. Much of this chapter's record therefore comes from other forms: broadcasts and speeches by the leaders, the Viceroy's official reports, dated letters, a press attaché's diary, a photographer's essay, and memoirs written afterwards from diaries or notes. Each eye is tagged with its real form, and the later memoirs are flagged.

The eyes are chosen so that each community and each new state speaks in its own voice. Nehru and Jinnah speak for the two governments, with Liaquat Ali Khan beside Nehru on the days they argued in public. Baldev Singh speaks for the Sikhs, whose homeland the Punjab line cut in two. Gandhi spends Independence Day fasting in Calcutta. Taunsvi, a Hindu, stays on in Lahore until November. Anis Kidwai, a Muslim widow, works in Delhi's camps. Penderel Moon, a British minister in a Pakistani princely state, tries to get Sikhs and Hindus out alive. Mountbatten and his press attaché watch from Government House, and Margaret Bourke-White photographs the columns going both ways.

The book takes no side on the questions still argued over: who was responsible, whether the timing was right, whether the line was fair, which killings came first. Where the eyes accuse one another, as Liaquat and Nehru did in September 1947, both accusations are reported as each man made it. The violence is described by its scale and by what the witnesses did and felt, not in detail.

Four clusters carry the chapter. 3 June brings the broadcasts. 14–15 August brings the midnight speeches and the celebrations, with Gandhi in a borrowed house in Calcutta. 16–17 August brings the boundary award, when every delegation found something to protest. Late August and September bring the trains, the camps, the Calcutta fast and the emergency in Delhi. Lord Wavell's journal, which ends with his departure in March 1947, falls before the period and is left out except as a link. So are novels such as Khushwant Singh's Train to Pakistan (1956) and the stories of Saadat Hasan Manto: they are powerful, but they are fiction.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. Pakistan celebrates independence on 14 August and India on 15 August. Under the Indian Independence Act both dominions came into being at the start of 15 August. Power was ceremonially transferred in Karachi on the morning of 14 August because Mountbatten had to be in Delhi for midnight. Some Muslim writers of the time also gave Hijri dates (15 August 1947 fell in Ramadan 1366 AH), and some Hindu and Sikh writers gave Vikram Samvat dates (1947 CE was 2004 VS). The entries here use the Gregorian date only.

eyes.name: Fikr Taunsvi (Ram Lal Bhatia)
eyes.role: Urdu poet, satirist and journalist, about 29, a Hindu Punjabi living and writing in Lahore
eyes.side: Punjabi Hindu; Urdu literary world of Lahore; became a refugee to India
eyes.where: Lahore (Sant Nagar and the Mall), then a refugee camp, then Khalsa College camp, Amritsar

waypoints.label: Crossing at Wagah by lorry, Nov 1947

eyes.vantage_label: inside Lahore as it became Pakistan, a Hindu who stayed as long as he could
eyes.authenticity: A dated journal kept from 9 August to 8 November 1947 and published in Urdu as Chhata Darya in 1948, within a year of the events. English translation by Maaz Bin Bilal, The Sixth River: A Journal from the Partition of India (Speaking Tiger, 2019). It is literary prose by a satirist and was shaped for publication, but it is one of very few non-fiction Partition journals written as events happened.
eyes.bio: Taunsvi was a Lahore Urdu writer with close Muslim friends, and he refused for weeks to believe he had to leave his city. His journal records curfews, rumours, arguments with friends and the news of trains, written by someone who kept insisting on the humanity of all sides. The 'sixth river' of the title is the river of blood added to the Punjab's five, an image he applies to every community's dead.

sources.title: Translator's introduction, Scroll.in
Excerpt: 11 August 1947, Scroll.in
Review, National Herald
The Sixth River: catalogue record, O.P. Jindal Global University

eyes.name: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi
eyes.role: Mahatma, 77, the moral leader of the Congress movement but holding no office; spent Independence Day in Calcutta
eyes.side: Indian nationalist; Hindu by faith, campaigning for peace between communities
eyes.where: Hydari Manzil, a derelict Muslim-owned house in Beliaghata, Calcutta; from 9 September, Delhi
eyes.vantage_label: peacemaker in a divided city, fasting rather than celebrating
eyes.form: dated letters, prayer speeches and press statements
eyes.authenticity: Gandhi kept no diary in these months. His dated letters, prayer-meeting speeches and statements were printed in The Collected Works of Mahatma Gandhi (vol. 89 covers August to November 1947). The digests here follow those texts as reported in secondary accounts.
eyes.bio: Gandhi chose to spend 15 August not in Delhi but in a riot-torn quarter of Calcutta, living in one house with H. S. Suhrawardy, the outgoing Muslim League premier of Bengal. When the killing in Calcutta started again on 31 August he began a fast that ended only when leaders of all communities promised peace. His letters show joy and dread side by side.

sources.title: 'The conditions on which Gandhi broke his last fast', The Wire
Beliaghata, Kolkata, Gandhi Heritage Portal
Freedom and Martyrdom, mkgandhi.org

eyes.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
eyes.role: 57, Vice-President of the Interim Government, then the first Prime Minister of India from 15 August 1947
eyes.side: Indian National Congress; Government of India
eyes.where: New Delhi; touring East and West Punjab in late August

waypoints.label: Sheikhupura and Lahore, end of Aug

eyes.authenticity: Public speeches and broadcasts, and letters printed in Selected Works of Jawaharlal Nehru (Second Series) and on the Nehru Archive with editorial footnotes. These are official and semi-official documents, not a diary.
eyes.bio: Nehru gave independent India its founding speech at midnight on 14–15 August. Two weeks later he was writing from camps in the Punjab, trying to count the uprooted and asking for doctors and lorries. His letters are frank about failures of order on both sides of the new border.

sources.title: To Lord Mountbatten, Lahore, 31 August 1947 (Nehru Archive)
To Vallabhbhai Patel, Camp Amritsar, 31 August 1947 (Nehru Archive)
Friendship with Pakistan, press statement, 16 September 1947 (Nehru Archive)
Constituent Assembly debates, 15 August 1947 (Lok Sabha digital library)

eyes.name: Muhammad Ali Jinnah
eyes.role: 70, President of the All-India Muslim League, then President of Pakistan's Constituent Assembly and first Governor-General of Pakistan
eyes.side: All-India Muslim League; Government of Pakistan
eyes.where: New Delhi until 7 August; then Karachi; Lahore in October–November
eyes.authenticity: Speeches and broadcasts printed in his collected speeches and statements (e.g. ed. Rafique Afzal). The 11 August speech survives in the Assembly record; for decades a recording was thought lost, and All India Radio handed recordings of his speeches to Pakistan in 2012. Public documents, not a diary.
eyes.bio: Jinnah had argued for Pakistan for seven years and won it in a shape he called moth-eaten. His speech of 11 August, about a state where religion would be each citizen's own concern, is still argued over in Pakistan. By late October he was speaking in Lahore to a city full of refugees.

sources.title: Speech of 3 June 1947 (text)
Jinnah announces the creation of Pakistan over All India Radio (F. W. Pritchett)
Selected speeches and statements of the Quaid-i-Azam, 1911–34 and 1947–48 (Open Library)

eyes.name: Liaquat Ali Khan
eyes.role: 52, General Secretary of the Muslim League, Finance Member of the Interim Government, then first Prime Minister of Pakistan
eyes.side: All-India Muslim League; Government of Pakistan
eyes.where: New Delhi, then Karachi; frequently in Lahore for joint conferences
eyes.form: official minutes and speeches (as recorded by others)
eyes.authenticity: Represented here through official records (Transfer of Power, vol. XII) and the editorial footnotes to Nehru's papers that summarise his 14 September 1947 speech. No diary; these are the record of what he said, kept partly by the other side.
eyes.bio: Liaquat sat opposite Nehru at the meetings where the boundary award was disclosed, and the two men toured the Punjab together trying to stop the killing. His speeches defended Pakistan's case as firmly as Nehru defended India's. Setting the two side by side shows how each government saw the same weeks.

sources.title: India: The Transfer of Power, vol. XII (archive.org text)
Friendship with Pakistan, 16 September 1947, with notes on Liaquat's 14 September speech (Nehru Archive)

eyes.name: Baldev Singh
eyes.role: 45, Sikh leader (Panthic party) and Defence Member of the Interim Government, then India's first Defence Minister
eyes.authenticity: Represented by his 3 June 1947 All India Radio broadcast and by his presence in official records. Thin compared with the other leaders; no diary is known.
eyes.bio: Baldev Singh spoke for the Sikhs on the night the plan was announced. Any line through the Punjab would split his community, its farmland and its holy places. His short broadcast accepted the plan and still hoped for a boundary that would keep Sikhs together.

sources.title: Nisid Hajari, Midnight's Furies, excerpt on the June 1947 broadcasts (Scroll.in)

eyes.name: Louis Mountbatten, Viscount (later Earl) Mountbatten of Burma
eyes.role: 47, last Viceroy of India, then Governor-General of the Dominion of India from 15 August 1947
eyes.where: Viceroy's House (from 15 August Government House), New Delhi; Karachi 13–14 August
eyes.vantage_label: principal actor, the British authority handing over power
eyes.authenticity: His weekly Viceroy's Personal Reports to London are printed in Mansergh and Moon (eds), India: The Transfer of Power 1942–7, vols X–XII. Personal Report No. 17, dated 16 August 1947, is document 489 in vol. XII. They were written by a principal actor partly to justify his own decisions, so his reasons and his feelings need to be read with that in mind.
eyes.bio: Mountbatten brought the date of transfer forward to 15 August 1947 and presided over the handover in both Karachi and Delhi. He also held back the boundary awards until after the celebrations. His reports describe the joy and the gathering violence in the same pages, as a man who meant to be seen as having done well.

sources.title: India: The Transfer of Power, vol. XII (archive.org text)

eyes.name: Alan Campbell-Johnson
eyes.role: 34, press attaché to the Viceroy, the first ever appointed to the post
eyes.where: Viceroy's House, New Delhi; with Mountbatten in Karachi 13–14 August
eyes.vantage_label: at the Viceroy's elbow, running the press
eyes.authenticity: A daily diary from March 1947 to June 1948, published as Mission with Mountbatten (Robert Hale, 1951). It was published while Mountbatten was alive and a loyal staff officer wrote it, so it is admiring and discreet. Entries here are dated by the events the diary covers. Where the digest relies on the well-known content of the book rather than a checked page, confidence is marked approx.
eyes.bio: Campbell-Johnson had served on Mountbatten's staff in the war, and he was brought to Delhi to deal with the world's press. He watched the 3 June plan presented, rode in the motorcades in Karachi and Delhi, and sat in on the long crisis meetings of September. His diary is the inside view of the Viceroy's House, cheerful in tone even when the news was not.

sources.title: Mission with Mountbatten (archive.org text)
Mission With Mountbatten, 1947 Partition Archive library

eyes.name: Anis Kidwai
eyes.role: About 41, Congress social worker from Barabanki; widowed in October 1947, then a volunteer in Delhi's refugee camps
eyes.where: Mussoorie, then Delhi: Purana Qila and Humayun's Tomb camps
eyes.vantage_label: relief worker among Muslim refugees in Delhi
eyes.form: memoir (written later) from a daily diary
eyes.authenticity: She kept a daily diary from 1947 to 1949 and turned it into the Urdu memoir Azadi ki Chhaon Mein, written in 1949 and published in 1974. The English translation by her granddaughter Ayesha Kidwai, In Freedom's Shade (Penguin, 2011), goes back to the diaries and restores passages left out of earlier editions. Exact days are seldom recoverable from the published text, so entries here are given by month.
eyes.bio: Anis Kidwai's husband, Shafi Ahmad Kidwai, was killed in Mussoorie in October 1947 while trying to keep the peace. She went to Delhi, and Gandhi told her that working for people who had lost everything would give her a reason to live. Her book is the women's-eye view of Delhi's camps, and of the work of recovering abducted women of every community.

sources.title: 'The unspeakable horrors of Delhi, 1947–49', Kafila
Feminism in India essay on Anis Kidwai
In Freedom's Shade, Penguin India

eyes.name: Penderel Moon
eyes.role: 42, British civil servant serving as Revenue Minister of Bahawalpur, a princely state that acceded to Pakistan
eyes.side: British official in Pakistani state service
eyes.vantage_label: official trying to move minorities out safely, on the Pakistan side
eyes.authenticity: Divide and Quit (1961) is a memoir written more than a decade later, drawing on his own notes and recollection, not a contemporary diary. Moon later co-edited the Transfer of Power documents and edited Wavell's journal, so he was also one of the historians of these events.
eyes.bio: Moon had resigned from the ICS in 1943 and came back to India at Wavell's invitation. In 1947 he was a minister in a Muslim princely state, responsible for getting its Hindus and Sikhs to India alive. His book is an unusually self-critical account by a British official of how order failed.

sources.title: Parvez Mahmood, 'A Tale of Two Massacres II', The Friday Times (draws on Divide and Quit)
Penderel Moon (Wikipedia)

eyes.name: Margaret Bourke-White
eyes.role: 43, LIFE staff photographer on assignment in India and Pakistan
eyes.where: Punjab roads and Delhi camps (Purana Qila)
eyes.vantage_label: foreign photographer on the refugee roads
eyes.authenticity: Her photographs ran in LIFE on 3 November 1947 as 'The Great Migration' (text by Lee Eitingon). Her book Halfway to Freedom (1949) is a memoir written afterwards. Exact dates of individual photographs are not given in the published captions, so entries here are given as ranges.
eyes.bio: Bourke-White had photographed Gandhi at his spinning wheel in 1946 and the liberated camps in Germany in 1945. In autumn 1947 she photographed Sikh, Hindu and Muslim columns on the Punjab roads and Muslims waiting in Delhi's Purana Qila. Her captions name the religion of each family, which the faces alone do not show.

sources.title: 'The Cost of Looking' on 'The Great Migration' (Boston University)
Mass Migration, India (LIFE Photo Collection, Google Arts & Culture)
Halfway to Freedom (Bauman Rare Books listing)

entries.headline: The Viceroy announces the plan on All India Radio
entries.digest: That morning Mountbatten put the plan for partition to the leaders, and that evening he presented it on All India Radio. Muslim-majority provinces could opt out of India, and the Punjab and Bengal assemblies would vote on dividing their provinces. A boundary commission would draw the line. His reports present it as the only plan all parties would accept, not as a choice he wanted.
entries.source_note: Broadcasts of 3 June 1947; Transfer of Power vol. XI (referred to in vol. XII introduction).

entries.headline: Nehru accepts division without joy
entries.digest: Nehru followed the Viceroy on the radio. He told listeners that Congress accepted the plan because the alternative was continued conflict. He said there was no joy in proposing to cut off parts of India, but that a smaller free India was better than a long struggle. He appealed for peace while the details were worked out.
entries.source_note: 3 June 1947 broadcasts; summarised in Hajari excerpt, Scroll.in.

entries.headline: Jinnah: the plan falls short, but must be weighed
entries.digest: Jinnah told Muslim listeners that the plan did not meet the League's view in some important respects, and that the League's council would have to decide whether to accept it as a compromise. He asked for calm and for no violence while it was weighed. He closed with the League's slogan for Pakistan.
entries.source_note: Text of the speech (advocatetanmoy.com); F. W. Pritchett's page on the broadcast; Hajari excerpt.

entries.headline: The Sikh spokesman accepts, hoping for a fair line
entries.digest: Baldev Singh spoke last for the Sikhs. He gave his community's assent without quibbling, though without enthusiasm. He hoped the boundary commission would draw a line that kept the Sikh people and their holy places together. Other Sikh leaders, including Master Tara Singh, were already saying they would resist any line that left them divided.
entries.source_note: Hajari, Midnight's Furies, excerpt on Scroll.in.

entries.headline: The Viceroy's press conference names a date
entries.digest: Campbell-Johnson had organised a large press conference, and he watched Mountbatten answer questions for hours without notes. Asked when power would be handed over, Mountbatten said it could be about 15 August. It was the first public hint of how short the time would be. The press attaché thought it a triumph, and he records none of the doubts that later critics raised.
entries.source_note: Mission with Mountbatten (1951), entry for 4 June 1947; date of press conference widely documented.

entries.headline: A letter to the King about hope
entries.digest: Two days after the broadcasts Mountbatten wrote to King George VI that India was full of new hope and expectancy. In the Punjab, meanwhile, the governor's reports were recording nightly killings in Lahore and Amritsar. The two kinds of report sit side by side in the official record.
entries.source_note: Quoted in Hajari excerpt (Scroll.in), citing Mountbatten's letter of 5 June.

entries.headline: A distressed note about Lahore burning
entries.digest: After a night of arson in Lahore's walled city, around Shahalmi Gate, Nehru wrote to Mountbatten that it was impossible to sit still while Lahore burned. He asked why the authorities could not act. The Punjab governor, Sir Evan Jenkins, replied with his own account of the riots and his own suspicions of who was behind them. That argument went on all summer.
entries.source_note: Hajari excerpt (Scroll.in); exact day of the note given as about 22 June.

entries.headline: A Lahore writer begins a journal
entries.digest: Taunsvi opened his journal in a Lahore full of rumour, with the boundary still unknown. Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims were all asking whether the city would go to India or to Pakistan. He wrote as a Hindu who loved the city and could not imagine leaving it, and who was angry with the leaders of every party.
entries.source_note: National Herald review: journal runs 9 August–8 November 1947.

entries.headline: After a 24-hour curfew, the streets are silent
entries.digest: Taunsvi went out on the morning after a full-day curfew and found the streets quiet and sluggish. Everyone moved warily, and he felt that every passer-by might be armed and waiting for an enemy. Neighbours who had known each other for years now looked at each other with distrust.
entries.source_note: Excerpt dated 11 August 1947, Scroll.in.

entries.headline: A speech on a state for all its citizens
entries.digest: Elected President of Pakistan's Constituent Assembly, Jinnah gave an unscripted address. He told members that in Pakistan people would be free to go to their temples, mosques or other places of worship. Religion, he said, had nothing to do with the business of the state, and in time Hindus would cease to be Hindus and Muslims Muslims in the political sense, as citizens of one state. Pakistanis still debate what he meant.
entries.source_note: Constituent Assembly of Pakistan proceedings, 11 August 1947; collected speeches.

entries.headline: Moving into a ruined house with Suhrawardy
entries.digest: Gandhi and H. S. Suhrawardy moved together into an abandoned house in a Hindu-Muslim border quarter of Calcutta. An angry Hindu crowd met them and demanded that Gandhi leave. That day he wrote to Satis Chandra Das Gupta that this might be the greatest risk he had ever taken.
entries.source_note: Letter to Satis Chandra Das Gupta, 13 August 1947; The Wire.

entries.headline: Handing over in Karachi
entries.digest: Mountbatten flew to Karachi on 13 August and the next morning addressed Pakistan's Constituent Assembly, transferring power. He and Jinnah then drove through the city together in an open car. The boundary awards had been ready by noon on the 13th, he noted, just too late for him to read before he left.
entries.source_note: Personal Report No. 17, 16 August 1947, paras 11, 57 (Transfer of Power XII, no. 489).

entries.headline: Riding behind an open car
entries.digest: Campbell-Johnson flew to Karachi with the Viceroy's party and followed the state drive through the city. He records the staff's worry about security for Jinnah and Mountbatten in an open car, and their relief when the drive passed off peacefully. That evening they flew back to Delhi for midnight.
entries.source_note: Mission with Mountbatten, entries for 13–14 August 1947.

entries.headline: Midnight: the tryst with destiny
entries.digest: Just before midnight Nehru told the Constituent Assembly that long ago India had made a tryst with destiny and that the time had come to redeem the pledge. As the world slept, he said, India would wake to life and freedom. He spoke of the end of an age, of the service of the millions, and of those suffering even as the country celebrated.
entries.source_note: Constituent Assembly debates, 14–15 August 1947.

entries.headline: The Governor-General's first message
entries.digest: Sworn in as Governor-General of Pakistan, Jinnah broadcast a message to the new nation. He saluted the birth of Pakistan and the sacrifices that had led to it. He promised fair treatment to the minorities, and he asked Pakistan's neighbours for goodwill and friendship.
entries.source_note: Collected speeches and statements, 15 August 1947 broadcast.

entries.headline: Independence Day spent fasting and spinning
entries.digest: Gandhi did not attend any celebration. He kept the day with a fast, prayer and spinning. The previous evening Suhrawardy had publicly admitted his share of responsibility for the killings of 1946, and Gandhi called that the turning point. That night crowds of Hindus and Muslims celebrated together in Calcutta streets that had been battlegrounds a year before.
entries.source_note: The Wire; Governance Now, 'Where was Mahatma Gandhi on the dawn of independence?'.

entries.place: Government House and Princes Park, New Delhi
entries.headline: The most remarkable day of his life
entries.digest: Mountbatten was sworn in as India's first Governor-General. That evening he went to the flag-raising at Princes Park near India Gate, where a crowd of several hundred thousand overwhelmed the ceremony. In his report he called it the most remarkable and inspiring day of his life, and he described the tumultuous scenes with evident delight.
entries.source_note: Personal Report No. 17 (Transfer of Power XII, no. 489); Salute, on the Princes Park ceremony.

entries.headline: A crowd that swallowed the parade
entries.digest: Campbell-Johnson saw the crowd break the barriers and fill the parade ground, so that the march past had to be abandoned. The Mountbattens could not get out of their carriage and watched from it as Nehru raised the flag. He notes a rainbow in the sky at the moment the flag went up, and the crowd took it as an omen.
entries.source_note: Mission with Mountbatten, entry for 15 August 1947; Salute (Col D. S. Sidhu) on the barricades and the abandoned march past.

entries.headline: Rejoicing, and unease
entries.digest: Writing to Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, Gandhi described the extraordinary rejoicing in Calcutta but said he felt uneasy. He was not sure the brotherhood in the streets would last. He wrote similar doubts to Vallabhbhai Patel.
entries.source_note: Letter to Amrit Kaur, 16 August 1947; The Wire.

entries.headline: The boundary awards handed to both governments
entries.digest: Mountbatten met the leaders of the two new dominions and gave them Sir Cyril Radcliffe's awards for the Punjab and Bengal. Each side had already complained about what it expected: Liaquat about Gurdaspur going to India, Patel about the Chittagong Hill Tracts going to East Pakistan. Mountbatten left it to the two governments to settle when and how the awards would be published. The same day he wrote his long report on the handover.
entries.source_note: Transfer of Power XII, nos. 487 (minutes), 488, 489, and intro.

entries.headline: Pakistan's objection to the Gurdaspur line
entries.digest: Liaquat attended for Pakistan. Before the meeting he had protested that giving most of Gurdaspur district to East Punjab would be a political decision rather than a judicial one. The award confirmed it. In the record he is the voice of Pakistan's grievance over the Punjab line, just as Patel and others voiced India's over the Bengal line.
entries.source_note: Transfer of Power XII, intro and nos. 428, 452, 454, 472, 485, 487.

entries.headline: The Sikhs find their homeland divided
entries.digest: Baldev Singh was among the leaders who received the awards. The Punjab line left Lahore, and Nankana Sahib, the birthplace of Guru Nanak, in Pakistan, and cut the Sikh farming districts in two. Every party at the table found something to protest. For the Sikh community the losses were among the heaviest.
entries.source_note: Transfer of Power XII (meeting of 16 August); Campbell-Johnson's account of the leaders present.

entries.headline: After the celebrations, gloom around the table
entries.digest: Campbell-Johnson recorded the change in mood when the leaders read the awards a day after the celebrations. Each delegation found fault with the line in different places. He thought this a kind of proof that Radcliffe had been impartial. He also noted the decision to publish the awards on the 17th.
entries.source_note: Mission with Mountbatten, entry for 16 August 1947.

entries.headline: Trains arriving in Lahore
entries.digest: Taunsvi wrote about the trains reaching Lahore station from the east carrying dead and wounded Muslims, and about attacks on trains of Hindus and Sikhs passing through Pakistan. He refused to keep a separate tally for each side. For him it was all one river of blood, flowing in both directions.
entries.source_note: National Herald review, citing the 25 August 1947 entry.

entries.headline: Nehru counts a million uprooted
entries.digest: After seeing Sheikhupura, which he called the worst devastation he had seen, Nehru wrote to Mountbatten from Lahore. About a million people had been uprooted, he wrote, and another million were in camps or homeless. Congress had opposed an exchange of populations, but people were moving anyway. The same day, writing to Patel from Amritsar, he asked for lorries, medicines and doctors for the hospitals.
entries.source_note: Letters to Mountbatten (Lahore) and to Patel (Camp Amritsar), 31 August 1947, Nehru Archive.

entries.headline: The peace in Calcutta breaks
entries.digest: An excited crowd of young Hindu men forced their way into Hydari Manzil, angry over a rumoured attack on a Hindu. Killing resumed in parts of the city the next day. The peace Gandhi had been celebrated for two weeks earlier seemed to have collapsed.
entries.source_note: The Wire (refers to 'the events of August 31 and September 1').

entries.headline: A fast until sanity returns
entries.digest: Gandhi began a fast that he said would end only when sanity returned to Calcutta. He wrote that if the rioting went on, there would be no point in his staying alive. Over the next two days leaders of the Hindu Mahasabha, of the Congress and of the Bengal Muslim League came to promise that they would work for peace.
entries.source_note: The Wire; Collected Works vol. 89.

entries.headline: The fast ends at a quarter past nine
entries.digest: Young men who had led the rioting came to Gandhi, surrendered and accepted any penalty. That evening a deputation of citizens from every community signed a pledge never again to allow communal strife in the city. Gandhi broke his fast at 9.15 p.m. In the next few days people brought in weapons and a peace corps was formed. Calcutta stayed largely quiet through the autumn.
entries.source_note: The Wire.

entries.headline: Asked to run the emergency
entries.digest: Delhi itself had now broken into killing, and Nehru and Patel asked Mountbatten to chair an Emergency Committee of the Cabinet. It handled curfews, troops, food and the refugee camps. A Ministry of Relief and Rehabilitation had just been created. Mountbatten took on the job, unusual for a constitutional Governor-General, and wrote about it with a sense of being needed.
entries.source_note: Mission with Mountbatten, prologue (Emergency Committee within three weeks of independence); Nehru Archive footnote on the relief ministry, 6 September.

entries.headline: Crisis staff work in a capital under curfew
entries.digest: Campbell-Johnson's diary moves from ceremony to the daily emergency meetings. He records curfews, rumours spreading faster than facts, the Mountbattens touring hospitals and camps, and the problem of getting accurate news to a frightened city and to the world's press. He was worried about how the killing would look abroad as well as about the killing itself.
entries.source_note: Mission with Mountbatten, entries for early September 1947.

entries.headline: Arriving in Delhi instead of the Punjab
entries.digest: Gandhi left Calcutta on 7 September intending to go on to the Punjab. He arrived in Delhi on the 9th to find the capital in turmoil and issued a statement to the press. He decided to stay in Delhi until it was at peace, and he began visiting the camps of Hindu and Sikh refugees from the west and of Delhi Muslims waiting to leave.
entries.source_note: The Wire (left 7 Sept, arrived Delhi 9 Sept, press statement).

entries.headline: Pakistan's Prime Minister speaks of hostile forces
entries.digest: Speaking in Lahore, Liaquat said that Pakistan faced hostile forces determined to strangle it at birth. He said Muslims in East Punjab were being killed by forces that were supposed to keep order, and that agreements were not being honoured. It was the case Pakistan's government was making to its own people and to the world.
entries.source_note: Summarised in the editorial note to Nehru's statement of 16 September 1947 (Nehru Archive).

entries.place: East and West Punjab roads; Purana Qila, Delhi
entries.headline: Photographing the columns from both sides
entries.digest: Bourke-White photographed refugee columns moving in both directions on the Punjab roads, Sikh convoys heading east and Muslim families heading west. In Delhi she photographed the thousands of Muslims camped inside the old walls of Purana Qila waiting for trains to Pakistan. Her later book describes how hard it was to photograph people at the worst moment of their lives.
entries.source_note: LIFE Photo Collection (Google Arts & Culture); Boston University essay on 'The Great Migration'; Halfway to Freedom (1949).

entries.headline: Nehru answers Liaquat
entries.digest: Nehru issued a press statement saying he was surprised and pained by Liaquat's speech. He denied that India treated Pakistan as an enemy. He admitted that forces of order had failed in some places, and said this had happened on both sides of the border. He said about a million and a quarter people had crossed in each direction, and he hoped the two dominions might one day draw close again.
entries.source_note: 'Friendship with Pakistan', press statement, 16 September 1947 (Nehru Archive).

entries.place: Rahim Yar Khan to the Indian border, Bahawalpur State
entries.headline: A Sikh column that did not get through
entries.digest: Moon helped organise the evacuation on foot of about 2,000 Sikhs from Rahim Yar Khan to India under a state army escort. The column set out on 26 September. On the night of 30 September, close to the border, it was betrayed and attacked. By Moon's estimate only some 600 to 700 reached safety. He records the state's arrest of the officer responsible, the man's escape, and the later recovery of most of the women who had been abducted. The account is sober, and it is also an admission of failure.
entries.source_note: Divide and Quit, as summarised in Parvez Mahmood, The Friday Times (10 March 2022).

entries.headline: News of Delhi calming, and quarrels among friends
entries.digest: Taunsvi recorded fresh attacks on trains and the abduction of women and girls. He also heard reports that Gandhi's appeals had calmed Delhi and that he might come to the Punjab. Rumours about Kashmir and armed men going there were going round Lahore. His Muslim friend Mumtaz came to apologise for an earlier argument, and Taunsvi set that small reconciliation down beside the larger news.
entries.source_note: Excerpt including the 9 October entry, Scroll.in (translator's introduction page).

entries.headline: Widowed, and sent to work
entries.digest: Anis Kidwai's husband Shafi Ahmad Kidwai was killed in Mussoorie, where he had stayed at his post trying to keep the peace. Grief-stricken, she went to Delhi and met Gandhi. He told her that working for those who had lost everything would give her a reason to live.
entries.source_note: Kafila; Feminism in India (month only).

entries.headline: Jinnah tells Lahore not to lose heart
entries.digest: Jinnah addressed a large public meeting in Lahore, a city now full of refugees from East Punjab. He spoke of Pakistan as the victim of a conspiracy, called on people not to panic, and asked them to protect the minorities and to work for the refugees. He promised that Pakistan would survive its first months.
entries.source_note: Collected speeches and statements (speech at Lahore, 30 October 1947); day not independently fetched.

entries.place: Purana Qila and Humayun's Tomb camps, Delhi
entries.headline: Inside the Muslim camps of Delhi
entries.digest: Kidwai worked in the crowded camps at Purana Qila and Humayun's Tomb, where Delhi Muslims waited either to go to Pakistan or to go home. She worked with volunteers from Jamia and with Subhadra Joshi and Sushila Nayar. Her diary records shortages, rumours, and the dread of families who did not know whether to stay. It also records the few Hindu and Sikh neighbours who came to help.
entries.source_note: Kafila; In Freedom's Shade (tr. Ayesha Kidwai, 2011).

entries.headline: A silent crowd listens to Jinnah
entries.digest: Taunsvi described a mass gathering in Lahore addressed by Jinnah, probably the meeting a few days earlier. Most of the crowd did not understand English, he noted, and they listened to the speech in silence. He watched a new nation listening to its founder, with himself as an outsider in the crowd.
entries.source_note: National Herald review, citing the 3 November 1947 entry.

entries.headline: 'The Great Migration' in LIFE
entries.digest: LIFE published Bourke-White's photographs as 'The Great Migration: Five Million Indians Flee for Their Lives'. For millions of Americans it was the first look at Partition. The captions identified people as Sikh, Hindu or Muslim, though the photographs themselves rarely could.
entries.source_note: LIFE, 3 November 1947, pp. 117–125, per Boston University essay.

entries.headline: The last entry, in a refugee camp
entries.digest: Taunsvi had finally left Lahore with other refugees, crossing at Wagah by lorry. His last entry was written in the camp at Khalsa College, Amritsar. He was now a refugee himself, with no idea where to go or how to live, and his hope for the city he had loved was gone.
entries.source_note: National Herald review; translator's introduction (Scroll.in).

convergences.label: The partition plan is broadcast
convergences.note: Four voices on one radio evening: the Viceroy presents the plan as the only one everyone would accept, Nehru accepts it without joy, Jinnah accepts it with reservations, and Baldev Singh accepts it while hoping for a line that keeps the Sikhs whole. Each is speaking to a different audience.

convergences.label: Karachi by day, Delhi at midnight
convergences.note: Power was handed over in Karachi in the morning and the tryst with destiny was spoken in Delhi at midnight. Meanwhile Gandhi sat in a half-wrecked house in Calcutta. Jinnah had set out his idea of a civic Pakistan three days earlier, on 11 August.

convergences.label: Independence Day
convergences.note: In Delhi the crowds overwhelmed the ceremony at Princes Park, and Mountbatten called it the most inspiring day of his life. In Calcutta Gandhi fasted and spun while Hindus and Muslims celebrated together in the streets. In Karachi Jinnah's first message as Governor-General promised fair treatment to the minorities.

convergences.label: The boundary award is disclosed
convergences.note: Every delegation at Government House found something to protest: Gurdaspur for Pakistan, the Chittagong Hill Tracts for India, Lahore and Nankana Sahib for the Sikhs. The same day in Calcutta, Gandhi wrote of rejoicing and unease.

convergences.label: Trains, camps and a broken peace
convergences.note: Nehru wrote from Lahore and Amritsar about a million people uprooted, and on the same day the Calcutta peace broke down around Gandhi. A week earlier Taunsvi had written about trains arriving full of dead and wounded in both directions.

convergences.label: Fast's end in Calcutta, emergency in Delhi
convergences.note: Calcutta had its pledge of peace on 4 September, and Delhi's crisis began within days. Gandhi went on to Delhi and stayed there.

convergences.label: Two governments, two accounts
convergences.note: Liaquat in Lahore and Nehru in Delhi each accused the other's forces of failing their duty, and each spoke of his own refugees. Days later, in Bahawalpur, Penderel Moon watched a column he had organised betrayed on the road to India.

convergences.label: After the flood
convergences.note: Jinnah had just spoken to a silent crowd in Lahore, and Taunsvi was in that crowd days before he became a refugee himself. That week LIFE showed America the columns, and Anis Kidwai was working in Delhi's Muslim camps.

ties.note: Leaders of the two successor states. They broadcast within minutes of each other on 3 June, and they spoke to their constituent assemblies within days of each other in August.
They toured the Punjab together and met at joint conferences in Lahore, and in September they exchanged public accusations through speeches and press statements.
Campbell-Johnson was Mountbatten's press attaché and wartime staff officer, and his diary is in part a record of Mountbatten's days.
After her husband's death Kidwai came to Gandhi in Delhi, and he set her to work in the refugee camps.
Mountbatten called Gandhi his 'one-man boundary force' for keeping Calcutta quiet while the Punjab burned. The phrase is widely attributed to him in late August 1947.
Moon later co-edited, with Nicholas Mansergh, the Transfer of Power documents in which Mountbatten's reports are printed, and he edited Wavell's journal.
Taunsvi stood in the Lahore crowd that heard Jinnah speak in English in late October or early November 1947, and he recorded its silence.
Bourke-White photographed Gandhi at his spinning wheel in 1946, and she interviewed him again shortly before his death in January 1948.
They sat at the same table on 16 August 1947, each finding the Punjab line unjust to his own people.

threads_out.note: Anis Kidwai's camps of 1947 were at Purana Qila and Humayun's Tomb. Ninety years earlier, in September 1857, the last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, had taken refuge at Humayun's Tomb and been captured there. On 16 August 1947 Nehru raised India's flag at the Red Fort, the palace from which Zafar had been taken.

The war shaped 1947. Britain was exhausted and in debt after 1945, and its new Labour government was set on leaving India quickly. Mountbatten and Campbell-Johnson came from the wartime South East Asia Command. Margaret Bourke-White had photographed the liberated camps in Germany in April 1945, two and a half years before she photographed the Punjab columns.

Mountbatten accepted the Japanese surrender at Singapore in September 1945. Guneeta Singh Bhalla founded the 1947 Partition Archive after seeing the video testimonies of bomb survivors at the Hiroshima Peace Memorial in 2008.

The 1947 Partition Archive, founded in 2010–11, has had volunteer 'citizen historians' record about 9,500 video testimonies from survivors in more than 500 cities in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and abroad. Stanford, Ashoka, LUMS and other universities hold copies. It is a living, many-eyed record that keeps growing, though it is testimony given decades later, not a diary of the time.
